top.line: Map an application like an agent, now with the compromise map: millions of attempts, no named compromise.
top.para: A remote code execution flaw hands the application's reach to anyone. An application behaviour policy lists reach, mandate, gap, barriers and per-row blast radius with a way back. The story site's compromise map, as of 20:50 UTC, finds millions of attempts and no organisation naming php2shell as the way in: lower likelihood, same blast radius.

in-short.line: Nine lines: an exploit hands over reach, map it, blast radius, three policies, bring-back, cuts, signals, and the silence.
in-short.para: An exploit gives an attacker the application's reach, so map it with the agent method, blast radius per row with a way back, plus decision and workflow policies. The restore question is the worst case if taken over anyway. Cut cheap rows, name signals. Millions of attempts but no named compromise lowers likelihood, not blast radius.

question.line: Patching is necessary but not sufficient; the restore question is what a full takeover would cost.
question.para: Councils, wikis and a national cyber centre took sites offline for php2shell. Bringing them back needs more than the fix: the incomplete-fix report was answered as an unrelated bug, but more flaws will come, and some sites run unfixable PHP versions. The question that lets someone sign off is what a takeover would cost, and few have written down its reach.

method.line: Reach, mandate, gap, barrier, footprint and blast radius all fit an application.
method.para: The words from footprint and blast radius carry over: reach is what the application process can do, mandate what the site is for, the gap the difference, barriers typed as boundary, setting, expectation or none, footprint read from logs, blast radius per row with a way back. Remote code execution turns a visitor's tiny grant into the application's reach.

three.line: Behaviour is the map; decision says who accepts each row; workflow says in what order.
three.para: The behaviour policy lists reach, mandate, gap, barriers and blast radius. The decision policy names who accepts open rows, who decides to restore, and which in-app actions need a person. The workflow policy orders the bring-back, patch to watch, and the application's own flows, such as storing a form before sending a confirmation.

example.line: An invented council site: ten rows, five cheap cuts, and a worst case reduced to defacement and database data.
example.para: A PHP content system on a cloud machine can typically write its code, use a full-rights database user, send mail, reach the internet and internal network, read instance credentials, hold admin sessions, see backups and hold third-party keys. Cutting code writes, mail, egress, credentials and backups, all configuration changes, shrinks a takeover to defacement and the database's data.

ours.line: Our static sites have a tiny run-time blast radius; it moved to the deploy pipeline.
ours.para: This newsroom and the PHP story site are static pages on GitHub Pages with no server process, database, mail or secrets of ours, so a takeover means false content with a redeploy as the way back. The blast radius moved to whoever controls deployment, which is why the rules of the game and the sidecar protect the pipeline.

bring-back.line: Seven steps: patch, map, write the mandate, cut cheap rows, name signals, decide with the likelihood, restore and watch.
bring-back.para: Patch to a fixed release or supplier build. Map each thing the application can do. Write its mandate with the owners. Cut egress, code writes, mail, credentials and mounted backups. Name each open row's trace, using the PHP site's detection signals. The named owner decides, weighing the compromise map's evidence. Restore and read the footprint, hourly then weekly.

new.line: The pieces are established practice; writing them as one policy per application, like agents, is the new part.
new.para: Least privilege, segmentation, threat modelling and business impact analysis are long established. The proposal is to write them as one policy per application in the same five words as for agents, with honest barrier types and per-row blast radius, so the same people, tools and reviews cover both, since both are code acting with a grant.

limits.line: Invented example; cuts reduce but do not fix; signals are not guarantees; facts as at 20:50 UTC; readings are mine.
limits.para: The worked example describes no real council. Cutting rows reduces blast radius but patching comes first. Signals are evidence a careful attacker can minimise. No third party's site was mapped. PHP facts are as the story site records them, the compromise map as of 20:50 UTC at v0.5.9. The three readings are the author's; the map assesses no risk.

sources.line: The memo, two method articles, the PHP story site's ledger, signals, fact-check and compromise map, and this site.
sources.para: Sources: the voice memos of 22 October 2026, the method in footprint and blast radius and the code you do not ship, the PHP story site's impact ledger, detection signals, fact-check and compromise map at v0.5.9, read at 21:06 UTC, and this site's own deployment, with related articles on PHP, mandates, policies and attack surface.

compromise.line: The compromise map: a wide search, millions of attempts, three vendors, one named attack, no named php2shell compromise.
compromise.para: The story site mapped 33 statements behind one claim as of 20:50 UTC: no named organisation says php2shell was the way in. It searched 184 vault sources, 773 watched pages, 3,444 news items and 295 probed sites. Attempts number millions; three vendors report exploitation without victims; one university reports a stopped attack; official signals show none exploited.

silence.line: Three readings: harder to exploit than it looks, compromises undisclosed, attackers unusually quiet.
silence.para: About 31 hours after disclosure, with millions of attempts and many unpatched hosts, no compromise is named. Exploitation may be harder than the score suggests; organisations may not disclose, with no obligation to do so quickly; attackers may be quiet. Either way, the silence lowers likelihood but not blast radius, and your own footprint is the only evidence about your site.

watching.line: Attention and exploitation may point at different places; a researcher will gather the week's flaws.
watching.para: php2shell drew government shutdown advice and national headlines, yet has no named victim, while CISA's catalogue filled with exploited flaws in VPN, mail and firewall devices, some zero-days. A researcher is collecting the past week's flaws and what is known of their exploitation, to test whether attention matches actual use with data.
